summary: This note covers several aspects of the Amazon rainforest: threats to indigenous territories from deforestation and ecocide, the effects of transportation and soy-driven development, and the region's extraordinary plant and animal biodiversity. It also summarizes the geological history of the Amazon drainage basin, including the Purus Arch and the formation of the Solimões Basin. The note appears to be a compiled wiki article with a repeated paragraph about plant biomass.
one_line: Overview of the Amazon rainforest covering indigenous peoples, deforestation rates, plant biodiversity, drainage history and species richness.
key_facts: Indigenous rainforest communities in the Peruvian Amazon continue to disappear as territories are destroyed by deforestation and ecocide.
The Urarina continue to struggle to fight for their cultural survival and the fate of their forested territories.
The needs of soy farmers have been used to justify many controversial transportation projects developing in the Amazon.
The mean annual deforestation rate from 2000 to 2005 was 22,392 km2 (8,646 sq mi) per year, 18% higher than the previous five years (19,018 km2 or 7,343 sq mi per year).
Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon declined significantly between 2004 and 2014, but has increased to the present day.
A 2001 study found a quarter square kilometer (62 acres) of Ecuadorian rainforest supports more than 1,100 tree species.
A 1999 study found one square kilometer (247 acres) of Amazon rainforest can contain about 90,790 tonnes of living plants.
The average plant biomass in the Amazon is estimated at 356 ± 47 tonnes per hectare.
An estimated 438,000 species of plants of economic and social interest have been registered in the Amazon region to date.
The total number of tree species in the Amazon region is estimated at 16,000.
During the mid-Eocene, the Amazon drainage basin was split along the middle of the continent by the Purus Arch.
As the Andes Mountains rose, a large basin enclosing a lake formed, now known as the Solimões Basin.
Within the last 5–10 million years, accumulating water broke through the Purus Arch, joining the easterly flow toward the Atlantic.
The Amazonian rainforests are the largest tract of tropical rainforest in the Americas.
One in ten known species in the world lives in the Amazon rainforest.
